guide.title: Read this as an upstream load-control story from a 2023 Discord Engineering report about a 2022-era system — not simply as a Cassandra-to-ScyllaDB database swap.
guide.problem: Discord's 2023 engineering report describes a 2022-era message store holding trillions of records on 177 Cassandra nodes. Skewed traffic created hot partitions, quorum reads spread their latency to neighboring queries, compaction fell behind, and JVM garbage-collection pauses turned routine operation into recurring on-call work.
guide.core_idea: Protect storage before replacing it: route a channel consistently to one stateless Rust data-service instance, coalesce concurrent reads for the same row into one database query, and bound concurrency. A safe migration gate is dual-write → token-range backfill with durable checkpoints → deterministic range counts/checksums plus shadow or sampled reads → mismatch repair → staged reads → source cutover → a tested rollback window. Keep Discord's observations separate from generic recommendations.
guide.outcome: Discord reported moving the message database from 177 Cassandra nodes to 72 ScyllaDB nodes in May 2022. The article reports historical-message reads changing from 40–125 ms p99 to 15 ms p99, inserts from 5–70 ms p99 to a steady 5 ms, and a custom migrator copying up to 3.2 million messages per second before a validated cutover. These are reported measurements for Discord's workload, hardware, configuration and time; they are not current-system claims or portable benchmark constants. As of 2026, Discord's post "How Discord Automates ScyllaDB Clusters at Scale" (2026-05-08) confirms ScyllaDB still stores messages, channels and servers across dozens of clusters and hundreds of nodes, with risky operations rehearsed on shadow clusters — the decision held, but no newer latency or node-count figures were published.
takeaways: A partition key distributes ownership, not demand. Channel-plus-time bucketing can bound partition size, but it cannot remove popularity skew: a hot channel or key may saturate one replica set. Name the unit explicitly—partition, bucket, token range and replica—and measure bytes, request concentration, cross-bucket reads and failure impact.

Storage reliability needs operational vocabulary. SSTables, compaction, tombstones and repair interact: a replica outage, missed repair or premature tombstone purge can produce stale or resurrected data. A quorum is a chosen consistency level, not a universal serializable guarantee; repair, compaction and tombstone-cleanup windows need explicit budgets and alerts.

The stateless Rust data-service and coalescer are a case-specific control point: consistent routing, bounded fan-in, deadlines, cancellation and fallback can protect either database engine. Treat this as a source-scoped Discord design observation, not a generic Rust or ScyllaDB performance guarantee.

Online migration needs an explicit evidence gate: dual-write → token-range backfill with durable checkpoints → deterministic counts/checksums plus shadow or sampled reads → mismatch repair → staged reads → source cutover → rollback window. Sampled comparison can expose divergence, but it does not prove equality without documented coverage and a repair path.

Data lifecycle is part of correctness. Test deletion, TTL, moderation, legal hold and retention across primary data, replicas, backups and migration snapshots; enforce tenant authorization and isolation, encryption and access-controlled restores. Do not put message contents in telemetry, and do not reuse Discord's source-specific result as universal best-practice wording.
review_lenses: Partition and failure vocabulary: distinguish partition, bucket, token range and replica; review hot-key percentiles alongside partition bytes, replica-outage behavior, repair SLA, tombstone grace and cleanup, compaction debt and consistency-level effects.

Migration gate: require dual-write ordering, durable checkpointed backfill, deterministic range counts or checksums, shadow/sample comparison, mismatch repair, a kill switch, staged reads, an explicit cutover authority and a tested rollback window.

Lifecycle and isolation: verify delete/TTL, moderation and legal-hold behavior in primary data, replicas, backups and migration snapshots; enforce tenant authorization and isolation, encryption, access logs and restore tests without placing message content in telemetry.

Evidence and wording: show a visible source/date label; mark 3.2m messages per second, node counts, p99s, the nine-day migration and the 99.9999% tombstone-heavy-range result as Discord-reported measurements with workload/hardware/configuration scope. Keep source-specific observations separate from best-practice prose; require a newer first-party source for current architecture and a matched remeasurement for portability. Before reusing any number, ask which Cassandra or Scylla versions, replication factor, consistency level, compaction strategy, hardware and partition distribution produced it; whether your maximum partition or bucket size and hot-channel percentile stay inside operational limits; what deterministic verification you have beyond sampled reads; whether deletion, moderation and retention obligations reach replicas, backups and migration snapshots; and whether repair and tombstone cleanup can finish inside your longest node-outage window.
